Testing yourself is not how you measure learning. It is how you cause it.
Re-reading feels like progress. Recalling without the page is progress.
Spacing the same hour of study across a week beats spending it in one sitting.
A little forgetting before review is not failure. It is what makes the review work.
If it feels easy, you are probably practising what you already know.
Mixing topics feels worse and works better than finishing one before the next.
You do not know something until you can explain it without looking.
Highlighting predicts almost nothing about what you will remember.
The gap between feeling sure and being right is where most learning hides.
Sleep is part of the study session, not the thing that follows it.
Answering slowly and getting it right beats recognising it instantly.
The best time to review is just before you would have forgotten.
Two short sessions on different days beat one long session on either of them.
Struggling to retrieve an answer strengthens it more than being shown it.
Reading a chapter twice is rarely worth as much as reading it once and closing it.
Explaining to someone who asks 'why' finds the gaps that nodding along hides.
Confidence and accuracy come apart most sharply on the material you skimmed.
Practising in the order the book uses is easier than the order you will be tested in.
The note you write in your own words is worth more than the passage you copied.
Interleaving old material with new costs a little speed and buys a lot of retention.
A question you got wrong and then corrected is worth more than one you got right.
Study until you can reproduce it, not until it looks familiar.
Distraction does not slow learning down so much as it stops it.
The point of a deadline is the spacing it forces, not the pressure it creates.
